**Jacob Gedleyihlekisa Zuma**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-6) (born 12 April 1942) is a South African politician who served as the fourth [president of South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_South_Africa "President of South Africa") from 2009 to 2018. Zuma was a former anti-[apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid "Apartheid") activist, member of [uMkhonto weSizwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UMkhonto_weSizwe "UMkhonto weSizwe"), and president of the [African National Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_National_Congress "African National Congress") (ANC) from 2007 to 2017. He is also the father-in-law of [Eswatini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eswatini "Eswatini") king [Mswati III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mswati_III "Mswati III").

Zuma was born in the rural region of [Nkandla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nkandla,_KwaZulu-Natal "Nkandla, KwaZulu-Natal"), which is now part of the [KwaZulu-Natal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KwaZulu-Natal "KwaZulu-Natal") province and the centre of Zuma's support base. He joined the ANC at the age of 17 in 1959 and spent ten years in [Robben Island Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_Security_Prison,_Robben_Island "Maximum Security Prison, Robben Island") as a [political prisoner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_prisoner "Political prisoner"). He went into exile in 1975 and was ultimately appointed head of the ANC's intelligence department. After the ANC was unbanned in 1990, he quickly rose through the party's national leadership and became deputy secretary general in 1991, national chairperson in 1994, and deputy president in 1997. He was the deputy president of South Africa from 1999 to 2005 under President [Thabo Mbeki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thabo_Mbeki "Thabo Mbeki"), [Nelson Mandela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela")'s successor. Mbeki dismissed Zuma on 14 June 2005 after Zuma's financial adviser, [Schabir Shaik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schabir_Shaik "Schabir Shaik"), [was convicted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schabir_Shaik_trial "Schabir Shaik trial") of making corrupt payments to Zuma in connection with the [Arms Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Arms_Deal "South African Arms Deal"). Zuma was [charged with corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma_corruption_charges "Jacob Zuma corruption charges") and was also acquitted on rape charges in the highly publicised [2006 trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma_rape_trial "Jacob Zuma rape trial"). He managed to retain the support of a [left-wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-wing_politics "Left-wing politics") coalition inside the ANC, which allowed him to remove Mbeki as ANC president in December 2007 at the ANC's [Polokwane elective conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/52nd_National_Conference_of_the_African_National_Congress "52nd National Conference of the African National Congress").

Zuma was elected president of South Africa in the [2009 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_South_African_general_election "2009 South African general election") and took office on 9 May. The criminal charges against him were formally withdrawn the same week. As president, he launched the R4-trillion National Infrastructure Plan and signed a controversial [nuclear power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power "Nuclear power") deal with the Russian government, which was blocked by the [Western Cape High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Cape_Division "Western Cape Division") in 2017. As a former member of the [South African Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Communist_Party "South African Communist Party"), he increasingly relied on [left-wing populist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-wing_populism "Left-wing populism") rhetoric, and in his 2017 [State of the Nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_the_Nation_Address_(South_Africa) "State of the Nation Address (South Africa)") address he announced a new policy of "radical economic transformation". Among the few policies implemented before the end of his presidency were [land expropriation without compensation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reform_in_South_Africa "Land reform in South Africa"), free [higher education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education_in_South_Africa "Higher education in South Africa"), a series of attempted structural reforms in key sectors involving restrictions on foreign ownership, and more stringent [black economic empowerment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Economic_Empowerment "Black Economic Empowerment") requirements. In the international arena, Zuma emphasised [South-South cooperation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South%E2%80%93South_cooperation "South–South cooperation") and [economic diplomacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_diplomacy "Economic diplomacy"). The admission of South Africa to the [BRICS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRICS "BRICS") grouping has been described as a major triumph for Zuma, and he has been praised for his [HIV/AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS "HIV/AIDS") policy.

Zuma's presidency was beset by controversy, especially during his second term. In 2014, the [Public Protector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Protector "Public Protector") found that Zuma had improperly benefited from state expenditure on upgrades to his [Nkandla homestead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nkandla_homestead "Nkandla homestead"), and in 2016, the Constitutional Court [ruled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Freedom_Fighters_v_Speaker_of_the_National_Assembly "Economic Freedom Fighters v Speaker of the National Assembly") that Zuma had failed to uphold the Constitution, leading to calls for his resignation and a failed [impeachment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impeachment_in_South_Africa "Impeachment in South Africa") attempt in the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_of_South_Africa "National Assembly of South Africa"). By early 2016, there were also widespread allegations, later investigated by the [Zondo Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zondo_Commission "Zondo Commission"), that the [Gupta family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_family "Gupta family") had acquired immense corrupt influence over Zuma's administration, amounting to [state capture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_capture "State capture"). Several weeks after Deputy President [Cyril Ramaphosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_Ramaphosa "Cyril Ramaphosa") was elected to succeed Zuma as ANC president in December 2017, the ANC [National Executive Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Executive_Committee_of_the_African_National_Congress "National Executive Committee of the African National Congress") recalled Zuma. After a fifth [vote of no confidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_of_no_confidence "Motion of no confidence") in [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_South_Africa "Parliament of South Africa"), he resigned on 14 February 2018 and was replaced by Ramaphosa the next day.

Shortly after his resignation, on 16 March 2018, the [National Prosecuting Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Prosecuting_Authority "National Prosecuting Authority") announced that it would reinstate corruption charges against Zuma in relation to the 1999 Arms Deal. He pleaded not guilty on 26 May 2021, but the trial was not scheduled to take place until early 2023. The trial has since been set for April 2025. In a separate matter, in June 2021, the [Constitutional Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_Court_of_South_Africa "Constitutional Court of South Africa") convicted [Zuma of contempt of court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma_contempt_of_court "Jacob Zuma contempt of court") for his failure to comply with a court order compelling his testimony before the Zondo Commission. He was sentenced to 15 months' imprisonment and was arrested on 7 July 2021 in [Estcourt, KwaZulu-Natal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estcourt "Estcourt"). However, he was released on [medical parole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_parole "Medical parole") two months later on 5 September. The high court rescinded his parole on 15 December. The parole was declared unlawful by the Supreme Court of Appeal, but it allowed the [Department of Correctional Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Correctional_Services_(South_Africa) "Department of Correctional Services (South Africa)") to consider whether to deduct the time spent under it from his sentence. On 11 August 2023, the Department of Correctional Services granted Zuma remission of his 15-month sentence.

## Early life

Zuma was born in [Nkandla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nkandla,_KwaZulu-Natal "Nkandla, KwaZulu-Natal"), [Natal Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natal_Province "Natal Province") (now part of the province of [KwaZulu-Natal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KwaZulu-Natal "KwaZulu-Natal")),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Gordin-7):1 and often moved around Natal and the suburbs of [Durban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durban "Durban") as a child.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-8) His father, Nobhekisisa, was a [policeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policeman "Policeman") who died when Zuma was five,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-9) and his mother, Geinamazwi, was a domestic worker.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Gordin-7):4[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Tromp-2018-10) His middle name, Gedleyihlekisa, means "one who smiles while causing you harm" in [Zulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zulu_language "Zulu language").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-veconomist-11) He did not receive formal schooling.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-12)

He has at least three brothers—Michael,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-13) Joseph,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-14) and Khanya[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-15)—and at least one sister—Velephi.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-16) Michael Zuma was employed by Khumbula Property Services, a construction company, and in 2011 admitted to using his elder brother Jacob's political status to secure a government contract for the company in exchange for a homestead in Nkandla.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-18)

## Anti-apartheid activism

### Imprisonment and exile

Zuma began engaging in anti-[apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid "Apartheid") politics at an early age and joined the ANC in 1959. He became an active member of [uMkhonto we Sizwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UMkhonto_we_Sizwe "UMkhonto we Sizwe") in 1962, two years after the ANC was banned.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-beresford-19) That year, he was arrested with a group of 45 recruits near [Zeerust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeerust "Zeerust") in western [Transvaal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transvaal_Province "Transvaal Province"), currently part of the [North West Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_West_Province_(South_Africa) "North West Province (South Africa)").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-sahistory-20) Zuma was convicted of conspiring to overthrow the apartheid government and was sentenced to ten years imprisonment, which he served on [Robben Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robben_Island "Robben Island") with [Nelson Mandela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela") and other notable ANC leaders also imprisoned during that time.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-sahistory-20) While imprisoned, Zuma was a [referee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referee_(association_football) "Referee (association football)") for prisoners association football games, organised by the prisoners own governing body, [Makana F.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makana_F.A. "Makana F.A.")[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-21)

After his release from prison, Zuma re-established ANC underground structures in Natal.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-anc-bio-22) He left South Africa in 1975 and was initially based in Swaziland where he met [Thabo Mbeki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thabo_Mbeki "Thabo Mbeki"). In Mozambique, he dealt with the arrival of thousands of exiles seeking military training in the wake of the 1976 [Soweto uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soweto_uprising "Soweto uprising"). He became a full member of the ANC [National Executive Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Executive_Committee_of_the_African_National_Congress "National Executive Committee of the African National Congress") in 1977,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-sahistory-20) and a member of the ANC's Politico-Military Council when it was formed in 1983.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-trewhela-23) He was also Deputy Chief Representative of the ANC in Mozambique, a post he occupied until the signing of the [Nkomati Accord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nkomati_Accord "Nkomati Accord") between the Mozambican and South African governments in 1984. After the Accord was signed, he was appointed as ANC Chief Representative in Mozambique.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-sahistory-20) In December 1986, the South African government requested that Mozambican authorities expel six senior members of the ANC, including Zuma. He was forced to leave Mozambique in January 1987, so he moved to the ANC headquarters in [Lusaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lusaka "Lusaka"), Zambia, where he was appointed Head of the ANC's underground structures, and shortly afterward was named chief of the intelligence department.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-sahistory-20)

Zuma was also a member of the [South African Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Communist_Party "South African Communist Party") (SACP).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-beresford-19) He joined in 1963, served briefly on the party's [Politburo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politburo "Politburo"),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-trewhela-23) and left in 1990.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-24)

### Return from exile

After the ANC was unbanned in February 1990, Zuma returned to South Africa on 21 March[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Tromp-2018-10) to begin the negotiations process.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-anc-bio-22) He was one of the first ANC leaders to return to South Africa for negotiations.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Tromp-2018-10) Later that year, he was elected unopposed as the ANC's Southern Natal Chairperson. Zuma, as a [Zulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zulu_people "Zulu people"), became known as a leading peace broker in Natal during the political violence of this period that was concentrated in that province, and arose largely from conflict between nationalist supporters of the then [Xhosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xhosa_people "Xhosa people")-dominated ANC and supporters of the Zulu nationalist[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-25)[Inkatha Freedom Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inkatha_Freedom_Party "Inkatha Freedom Party") (IFP).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Tromp-2018-10) He is also credited with having expanded the ANC's Zulu support base in Natal.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-26) At the ANC's [July 1991 elective conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/48th_National_Conference_of_the_African_National_Congress "48th National Conference of the African National Congress"), Zuma stood for the post of ANC Secretary-General and lost to [Cyril Ramaphosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_Ramaphosa "Cyril Ramaphosa"), but was elected Deputy Secretary-General, comfortably beating [Alfred Nzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Baphethuxolo_Nzo "Alfred Baphethuxolo Nzo") and [Popo Molefe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popo_Molefe "Popo Molefe") in a vote.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Wren-1991-27)

In the [1994 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_South_African_general_election "1994 South African general election"), South Africa's first democratic election, Zuma stood as the ANC's candidate for the [premiership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_(South_Africa) "Premier (South Africa)") of his newly constituted home province, [KwaZulu-Natal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KwaZulu_Natal "KwaZulu Natal").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-sahistory-20) The ANC rose to power in the elections, with Mandela elected president and Mbeki his deputy, but lost KwaZulu-Natal to the IFP. Zuma became a [member of the executive council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_the_Executive_Council "Member of the Executive Council") (MEC) for economic affairs and tourism in KwaZulu-Natal.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-anc-resignation-stmt-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-29) In December 1994, he was elected [ANC provincial chairperson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provincial_Chairperson_of_the_African_National_Congress "Provincial Chairperson of the African National Congress") for KwaZulu-Natal, and at the ANC's [1994 elective conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/49th_National_Conference_of_the_African_National_Congress "49th National Conference of the African National Congress") he was elected national chairperson, beating [Pallo Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pallo_Jordan "Pallo Jordan") and [Jeff Radebe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Radebe "Jeff Radebe") by a large margin.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Namibian-1994-30) He held both positions until 1997, having been re-elected provincial chairperson in 1996.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-sahistory-20)

## Rise to the presidency

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/The_Vice_President_Shri_Bhairon_Singh_Shekhawat_meeting_the_Deputy_President_of_South_Africa_Mr._Jacob_Zuma_in_Johannesburg_on_April_28%2C_2004.jpg/250px-The_Vice_President_Shri_Bhairon_Singh_Shekhawat_meeting_the_Deputy_President_of_South_Africa_Mr._Jacob_Zuma_in_Johannesburg_on_April_28%2C_2004.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Vice_President_Shri_Bhairon_Singh_Shekhawat_meeting_the_Deputy_President_of_South_Africa_Mr._Jacob_Zuma_in_Johannesburg_on_April_28,_2004.jpg)

Zuma with the Indian Vice President [Bhairon Singh Shekhawat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhairon_Singh_Shekhawat "Bhairon Singh Shekhawat") in [Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg "Johannesburg"), 2004

### Deputy presidency

Zuma was elected deputy president of the ANC at the party's [50th National Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/50th_National_Conference_of_the_African_National_Congress "50th National Conference of the African National Congress") in [Mafikeng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mafikeng "Mafikeng") in December 1997, and was subsequently appointed deputy president of South Africa in June 1999, pursuant to the [1999 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_South_African_general_election "1999 South African general election").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-sahistory-20) Zuma served under newly elected President Mbeki and was the chief mediator in the [Burundi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burundi "Burundi") peace process,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-31) in which he worked with Ugandan president [Yoweri Museveni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoweri_Museveni "Yoweri Museveni"), who chaired the Great Lakes Regional Initiative, a grouping of regional presidents overseeing the peace process in Burundi.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-32)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Bulelani_Ngcuka.png/250px-Bulelani_Ngcuka.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bulelani_Ngcuka.png)

Under [Bulelani Ngcuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulelani_Ngcuka "Bulelani Ngcuka"), the NPA opened its investigation into Zuma.

In late 2002, the [National Prosecuting Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Prosecuting_Authority "National Prosecuting Authority") (NPA) announced that Zuma was one of several ANC politicians under investigation by the [Scorpions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scorpions_(South_Africa) "Scorpions (South Africa)") for corruption related to the R30-billion [Arms Deal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Arms_Deal "South African Arms Deal"), a major defence procurement package which the government had signed months after Zuma's appointment to the deputy presidency.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Bruce-2008-33) In August 2003, however, National Director of Public Prosecutions (NDPP) [Bulelani Ngcuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulelani_Ngcuka "Bulelani Ngcuka") told the media that the NPA had a "prima facie case of corruption" against Zuma but had decided not to prosecute on the basis that the case was unlikely to be won.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Bruce-2008-33) A highly public spat ensued between Zuma allies and Ngcuka, who was accused by [Moe Shaik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moe_Shaik "Moe Shaik") and [Mac Maharaj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mac_Maharaj "Mac Maharaj") of having been an apartheid spy, an accusation later dismissed by the specially appointed Hefer Commission.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-34) Zuma laid a misconduct complaint against Ngcuka with the [Public Protector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Protector "Public Protector"), [Lawrence Mushwana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Mushwana "Lawrence Mushwana"), who in May 2004 found that Ngcuka's statement to the media had been "unfair and improper".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-36)

Mbeki and Zuma were both re-elected in the [2004 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_South_African_general_election "2004 South African general election"), but on 14 June 2005, Mbeki removed Zuma from his post as deputy president following [the conviction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schabir_Shaik_trial "Schabir Shaik trial") of Zuma's associate, [Schabir Shaik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schabir_Shaik "Schabir Shaik"), for making underhanded payments to Zuma in relation to the Arms Deal.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-37) Mbeki told a joint sitting of [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_South_Africa "Parliament of South Africa") that "in the interest of the honourable Deputy President, the government, our young democratic system and our country, it would be best to release the honourable Jacob Zuma from his responsibilities".[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-sacked-38) Zuma also resigned as a member of Parliament.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-sacked-38)

His successor as deputy president of South Africa was [Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phumzile_Mlambo-Ngcuka "Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka"), Ngcuka's wife. Mlambo-Ngcuka had been minister of minerals and energy since 1999. Her appointment was booed publicly at ANC rallies by Zuma supporters, including at a [Women's Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Women's_Day "National Women's Day") event in [Utrecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utrecht,_KwaZulu-Natal "Utrecht, KwaZulu-Natal"), KwaZulu-Natal.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-39)

### First corruption indictment

Further information: [Jacob Zuma corruption charges First indictment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma_corruption_charges#2005%E2%80%932006:_First_indictment "Jacob Zuma corruption charges")

Soon after Zuma's dismissal, the NPA announced its intention to instate formal corruption charges against him.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-40) He was served with a provisional [indictment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indictment "Indictment") on fraud and corruption charges in November 2005, mirroring the indictment earlier served on Shaik.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-longpath22-41) However, the NPA was unprepared to serve the final indictment and filed an application for postponement. On 20 September 2006, the [Pietermaritzburg High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pietermaritzburg_High_Court "Pietermaritzburg High Court") dismissed the application, and when the NPA indicated that it was not prepared to proceed with the trial, the matter was stricken off.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-SABC2006-09-20222-42)

### Rape trial

Main article: [Jacob Zuma rape trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma_rape_trial "Jacob Zuma rape trial")

In December 2005, Zuma was charged with raping a 31-year-old woman, known to the public by the pseudonym Khwezi.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Pather-2016-43) The incident allegedly occurred on 2 November 2005 at Zuma's home in [Forest Town, Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Town,_Gauteng "Forest Town, Gauteng").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Mail_&_Guardian-2006-44) When the trial began on 6 March 2006, Zuma pleaded not guilty, claiming that he and Khwezi had [consensual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consensual_sex "Consensual sex") sex.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Mail_&_Guardian-2006-44) He was acquitted on 8 May 2006 following a highly publicised trial.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Humphreys-2006-45) Zuma's admission was controversial, as he stated that he had not used a condom while having sex with Khwezi, despite knowing she was [HIV-positive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV-positive "HIV-positive") and having been, as deputy president, the head of the National AIDS Council and Moral Regeneration Campaign. He told the court that he had taken a shower after the act, claiming that doing so reduced the risk of [HIV transmission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV_transmission "HIV transmission").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-SA's_Zuma_showered_to_avoid_HIV-46) The South African comic strip _[Madam & Eve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madam\_&\_Eve "Madam & Eve"),_ and political cartoonist [Zapiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zapiro "Zapiro"), repeatedly lampooned Zuma for his testimony, and Zuma now always appears under a showerhead in Zapiro cartoons.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-47)

### Continued popularity

Although Zuma had been fired as national deputy president, he retained the ANC deputy presidency, and internal factions began to coalesce around him and Mbeki. Between 2005 and 2007, their rivalry deepened into what Susan Booysen called "a brutal and all-consuming disagreement between two major ANC groupings".[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Booysen-2011-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-49)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Gevisser-2007-50) Although the corruption and rape allegations were considered politically damaging,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-SA's_Zuma_showered_to_avoid_HIV-46)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-The_Guardian-2006-51) Zuma continued to enjoy considerable support from [left-wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-wing_politics "Left-wing politics") elements of the ANC, especially the [ANC Youth League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_National_Congress_Youth_League "African National Congress Youth League") under [Fikile Mbalula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fikile_Mbalula "Fikile Mbalula"), and from the ANC's partners in the [Tripartite Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tripartite_Alliance "Tripartite Alliance"), the SACP, and the [Congress of South African Trade Unions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_South_African_Trade_Unions "Congress of South African Trade Unions") (COSATU).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-52)[Blade Nzimande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blade_Nzimande "Blade Nzimande") of the SACP and [Zwelinzima Vavi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zwelinzima_Vavi "Zwelinzima Vavi") of COSATU were among Zuma's chief organisers and most vocal supporters (though both recanted their support years later).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Du_Toit-2017-53) Vavi and Youth League leader [Julius Malema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Malema "Julius Malema") later said that they were prepared to "kill for Zuma".[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-dmc3-54)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-55) Nzimande and his SACP comrade [Gwede Mantashe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwede_Mantashe "Gwede Mantashe") warned that the corruption trial would endanger public stability if it went ahead,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-dmc3-54) although there were reports that support for Zuma had caused a rift within the SACP.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-56)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-57) While Zuma's political strength was at least partly based on his relationships within intra-party politics and Mbeki's lack of popularity with the left wing, he also had a large Zulu support base,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Gevisser-2007-50) and one analyst argued that his supporters' loyalty was partially rooted in a traditionalist Zulu loyalty.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-58)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Zuma-court-crowd.jpg/250px-Zuma-court-crowd.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zuma-court-crowd.jpg)

A crowd of supporters and curious onlookers outside the [Johannesburg High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg_High_Court "Johannesburg High Court") during the rape trial

Zuma's supporters publicly expressed the view that his dismissal and prosecution were the result of a political conspiracy by Mbeki, who they said had sought to oust Zuma to entrench their dominance in the ANC.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Booysen-2011-48)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-59) Zuma's court appearances on the corruption charges drew large crowds of supporters (on one estimate, up to 10,000 at a time),[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Robinson-2006-60) who, on one occasion, burned T-shirts with Mbeki's picture on them, which the ANC leadership condemned.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-61) Zuma became known for singing the apartheid-era struggle song "_[Umshini wami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umshini\_wami "Umshini wami")_" (English: _Bring Me My Machine Gun_) with his supporters during these informal rallies.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-62)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-63) Likewise, during the rape trial, Zuma supporters gathered outside the courthouse and sometimes clashed with smaller groups of anti-rape protesters.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Humphreys-2006-45)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-64)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-The_Guardian-2006-51) Zuma supporters were seen carrying posters questioning Khwezi's integrity, burning photos of her, and on one occasion throwing stones at a woman that they mistook for her.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Mail_&_Guardian-2006-44)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-65)

By October 2008, Zuma had been acquitted of rape[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Humphreys-2006-45)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-66) and was no longer subject to corruption charges. However, this did little to lighten the rivalry between Mbeki and Zuma. A _[Mail & Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail\_&\_Guardian "Mail & Guardian")_ analysis stated:

> The political damage [of events of recent months] is incalculable, with the ruling African National Congress now an openly divided and faltering movement. This has had a [domino effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domino_effect "Domino effect") on the South African Communist Party and the Congress of South African Trade Unions, which have floundered and fractured in the face of damaging charges against a man they ardently backed as the country's next president. The trial has been fought against the backdrop of a bitter succession war between Mbeki and Zuma. Both have been fatally wounded. Mbeki's support in the ANC has crumbled... But even Zuma's most diehard supporters privately acknowledge that he cannot now be president...[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Robinson-2006-60)

### Defamation lawsuits

By early 2006 during the rape trial, Zuma and his supporters complained of a concerted media plot to discredit him and harm his political career.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-IOL-2006-67) In March, he appointed a legal team, including former [Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(South_Africa) "Conservative Party (South Africa)") politician Jurg Prinsloo and advocate Wycliffe Mothuloe, to fight his "crucifixion by the media".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Mail_&_Guardian-2006-44)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-IOL-2006-67) Among his targets was the _Sowetan,_ whom he told that the media, at the instruction of Ngcuka of the NPA and former Justice Minister [Penuell Maduna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penuell_Maduna "Penuell Maduna"), was trying to "crucify" him. The newspaper had printed the interview under the headline "I'm like Christ – Zuma".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-IOL-2006-67) In June and July 2006, Zuma filed a series of [defamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defamation "Defamation") lawsuits against various South African media outlets for publishing content that allegedly besmirched his public profile in the form of cartoons, commentary, photos and parody pieces. The defendants included the _[Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Star\_(South\_Africa) "The Star (South Africa)")_ (sued for R20 million), [_Rapport_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapport_(newspaper) "Rapport (newspaper)") (R10 million), [Highveld Stereo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/94.7_Highveld_Stereo "94.7 Highveld Stereo") (R7 million), the _[Sunday Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday\_Times\_(South\_Africa) "Sunday Times (South Africa)")_ (R6 million), the _[Citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Citizen\_(South\_Africa) "The Citizen (South Africa)")_ (R5 million), the _Sunday Sun_ (R5 million), the _[Sunday Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday\_Independent\_(South\_Africa) "Sunday Independent (South Africa)")_ (R5 million), and the _Sunday World_ (R5 million).[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-68)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-69) Zuma said in 2005:

> For a period of five years my person has been subjected to all types of allegations and innuendo, paraded through the media and other corridors of influence without these allegations having being[_[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic "Sic")_] tested. I have thereby been denied my constitutional right to reply and defend myself.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-70)

In December 2008, Zuma sued Zapiro for R7 million over his controversial [rape of Lady Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rape_of_Lady_Justice_cartoon_controversy "Rape of Lady Justice cartoon controversy") cartoon,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-dmc3-54) bringing the total value of the defamation lawsuits to at least R70 million, an unprecedented figure in South African law.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-71) Many of the suits were withdrawn or settled out of court. _Rapport_ settled for R50,000 over a defamatory reader's letter, and the British _[Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_ newspaper also paid Zuma substantial damages over defamatory statements.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-72)

### Election as ANC president

Further information: [52nd National Conference of the African National Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/52nd_National_Conference_of_the_African_National_Congress "52nd National Conference of the African National Congress")

As per party tradition, Zuma was in line to succeed Mbeki as head of the party. However, by April 2007[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Gevisser-2007-50)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-73)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-74) it was clear that Mbeki intended to run for a third term as ANC president. Even though he was prohibited by the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_South_Africa "Constitution of South Africa") from standing again for the national presidency, the ANC lacks internal term limits. Zuma gained the support of five of the nine provincial ANC branches when they nominated candidates at their provincial congresses in late 2007.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Du_Toit-2017-53)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-75)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-76) He became the favourite to win the presidency and became the ANC's presidential candidate in the [2009 elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_South_African_general_election "2009 South African general election"). While the ANC was extremely likely to win regardless of its candidate, there were reports that Zuma's support base and left-wing alliances unnerved international and domestic investors.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-77)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-78)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-mcgreal2-79)

On 18 December 2007, at the ANC's [52nd National Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/52nd_National_Conference_of_the_African_National_Congress "52nd National Conference of the African National Congress") in [Polokwane, Limpopo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polokwane "Polokwane"), Zuma was elected ANC president, beating Mbeki with 2,329 votes to 1,505.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-80)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Jacob_Zuma_in_2008.jpg/250px-Jacob_Zuma_in_2008.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jacob_Zuma_in_2008.jpg)

Zuma in June 2008

### Second corruption indictment

Further information: [Jacob Zuma corruption charges § Second indictment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma_corruption_charges#2007%E2%80%932009:_Second_indictment "Jacob Zuma corruption charges")

Just over a week after the Polokwane conference, the NPA reinstated charges against Zuma and served him an indictment to stand trial on 12 fraud charges, two corruption charges, and one charge each of [racketeering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racketeering "Racketeering") and [money laundering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Money_laundering "Money laundering").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-81)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-iol.co.za-82) According to the Constitution, he would have been rendered ineligible for the national presidency had he been convicted and sentenced to imprisonment. However, on 12 September 2008, the charges were declared unlawful on a technicality. The presiding judge also expressed a belief that the charges had been the result of a political conspiracy against Zuma.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-dismiss22-83)

Although this judgement was later overturned by the appellate court, the Zuma-aligned ANC [National Executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Executive_Committee_of_the_African_National_Congress "National Executive Committee of the African National Congress"), as elected at the Polokwane conference, immediately "recalled" Mbeki, asking him to resign as national president.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-ioltimeline22-84) Mbeki, seeking to avoid a protracted dispute, did so, and was replaced by newly elected ANC Deputy President [Kgalema Motlanthe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kgalema_Motlanthe "Kgalema Motlanthe"), who led an interim administration while Zuma campaigned for the 2009 election.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-85)

In January 2009, the [Supreme Court of Appeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Appeal_(South_Africa) "Supreme Court of Appeal (South Africa)") found that the charges against Zuma were not unlawful, contrary to the ruling of the lower court. However, the NPA formally withdrew the charges in the same week that Zuma was inaugurated as national president,[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-ioltimeline22-84) citing apparent evidence of prosecutorial misconduct in the so-called [spy tapes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Prosecuting_Authority#%22Spy_tapes%22_allegations "National Prosecuting Authority").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Mail_&_Guardian-86)

### Release of Shaik on parole

In March 2009, Shaik was controversially released from prison on [medical parole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compassionate_release "Compassionate release"), just over two years into his 15-year sentence. Earlier the same week, Zuma had said publicly that as national president he would pardon Shaik on medical grounds, and denied having played any role in Shaik's release.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Bearak-2009-87) Shaik had applied for a presidential pardon in April 2008 when Mbeki was president, and he continued to lobby for a pardon during Zuma's presidency, saying it was unfair that he had been convicted while neither Zuma nor the implicated arms company had been taken to trial.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-88)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-89)

## President of South Africa (2009–2018)

Main article: [Presidency of Jacob Zuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Jacob_Zuma "Presidency of Jacob Zuma")

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/2009_news_seller_Capetown_3563345045.jpg/250px-2009_news_seller_Capetown_3563345045.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2009_news_seller_Capetown_3563345045.jpg)

A [Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Town "Cape Town") news vendor displays the headline "Zuma Dawn" on 10 May 2009.

The ANC won the national election on 22 April 2009 by a slightly diminished majority of 65.90%, with Zuma having campaigned under the theme "Continuity and Change".[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Landsberg-2012-90)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-91) His appointment was [formalised by Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_South_African_presidential_election "2009 South African presidential election") on 6 May, and he was sworn in as president of South Africa on 9 May 2009.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-ioltimeline22-84)

### Failure to disclose assets

As president and therefore a member of cabinet, Zuma was required by the government's ethics code to declare his financial interests within 60 days of taking office. In March 2010, nine months after taking office, South African media reported that he had failed to do so. Opposition parties and the ANC's Tripartite Alliance partner COSATU urged Zuma to disclose his interests, and the opposition Democratic Alliance (DA) called for an investigation by the [Public Protector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Protector "Public Protector").[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-92) ANC spokesperson Brian Sokutu explained that Zuma constituted a "special case" because of his "large family", which complicated the process.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Sunday_Times-2010-93) The ANC distanced itself from Sokutu's statement[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Sunday_Times-2010-93) and Zuma filed the disclosure later that week.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-94)

### Domestic policy

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Zuma_Stadium_Tour%2C_2009_World_Economic_Forum_on_Africa.jpg/250px-Zuma_Stadium_Tour%2C_2009_World_Economic_Forum_on_Africa.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zuma_Stadium_Tour,_2009_World_Economic_Forum_on_Africa.jpg)

Zuma (centre) on a tour of [Green Point Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Point_Stadium "Green Point Stadium") in June 2009, in preparation for the [2010 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_FIFA_World_Cup "2010 FIFA World Cup")

#### Radical economic transformation

As a former member of the SACP, Zuma has described himself as a socialist[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-mcgreal2-79) and became president with the support of a left-wing coalition.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-mcgreal2-79)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-95) Analysts have claimed that he has bolstered [populism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Populism "Populism") in South Africa.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-96)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-97) From 2017, at the tail-end of his presidency, his rhetoric and policy priorities became more leftist under what is known as the "radical economic transformation" (RET) programme of the ANC of this period. Zuma announced the new focus on RET during his February 2017 [State of the Nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_the_Nation_Address_(South_Africa) "State of the Nation Address (South Africa)") address.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-98) Later that year, he explained that RET had been adopted as ANC policy and therefore as government policy, and defined it as a "fundamental change in the structures, systems, institutions and patterns of ownership and control of the economy, in favour of all South Africans, especially the poor".[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Paton-2017-99) The RET policy was controversial,[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-100) and some critics claimed that it had popular political appeal but lacked substance.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-101)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Rudin-2017-102) Others claimed that it was used to defend "rent-seeking practices"[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-103) and the influence of the [Gupta family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_family "Gupta family") on Zuma's administration.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-104)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-105) Zuma claimed that critics of his politics were agents of "[white monopoly capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_monopoly_capital "White monopoly capital")".[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Rudin-2017-102)

#### Economic reform and spending

Zuma was inaugurated in South Africa at during the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis") and the first [recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recession "Recession") in South Africa since the end of apartheid.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Shipalana-2017-106) Upon taking office, he established the [National Planning Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Planning_Commission_of_South_Africa "National Planning Commission of South Africa") under the office of the presidency which was chaired by Minister [Trevor Manuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Manuel "Trevor Manuel"). It was responsible for developing the [National Development Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Development_Plan "National Development Plan"), which was adopted by Zuma's cabinet in 2012.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-107)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-108) Other major initiatives included the Independent Power Producers Procurement Programme, which was launched in 2011 amid [electricity generation shortfalls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_energy_crisis "South African energy crisis") at state energy utility [Eskom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eskom "Eskom"), and a R4-trillion National Infrastructure Plan launched in 2012.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-109)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-110)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-111) Zuma expressed support for expanding South Africa's [nuclear power programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_power_in_South_Africa "Nuclear power in South Africa"), particularly for a nuclear deal with Russian nuclear agency [Rosatom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosatom "Rosatom") which concluded in September 2014 but was ruled unlawful by the [Western Cape High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Cape_Division "Western Cape Division") in 2017.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Business_Day-2019-112)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Maughan-2019-113)

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/%D0%92%D1%81%D1%82%D1%80%D0%B5%D1%87%D0%B0_%D0%92%D0%BB%D0%B0%D0%B4%D0%B8%D0%BC%D0%B8%D1%80%D0%B0_%D0%9F%D1%83%D1%82%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%B0_%D1%81_%D0%9F%D1%80%D0%B5%D0%B7%D0%B8%D0%B4%D0%B5%D0%BD%D1%82%D0%BE%D0%BC_%D0%AE%D0%90%D0%A0_%D0%94%D0%B6%D0%B5%D0%B9%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B1%D0%BE%D0%BC_%D0%97%D1%83%D0%BC%D0%BE%D0%B9_1.jpg/250px-%D0%92%D1%81%D1%82%D1%80%D0%B5%D1%87%D0%B0_%D0%92%D0%BB%D0%B0%D0%B4%D0%B8%D0%BC%D0%B8%D1%80%D0%B0_%D0%9F%D1%83%D1%82%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%B0_%D1%81_%D0%9F%D1%80%D0%B5%D0%B7%D0%B8%D0%B4%D0%B5%D0%BD%D1%82%D0%BE%D0%BC_%D0%AE%D0%90%D0%A0_%D0%94%D0%B6%D0%B5%D0%B9%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B1%D0%BE%D0%BC_%D0%97%D1%83%D0%BC%D0%BE%D0%B9_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%D0%92%D1%81%D1%82%D1%80%D0%B5%D1%87%D0%B0_%D0%92%D0%BB%D0%B0%D0%B4%D0%B8%D0%BC%D0%B8%D1%80%D0%B0_%D0%9F%D1%83%D1%82%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%B0_%D1%81_%D0%9F%D1%80%D0%B5%D0%B7%D0%B8%D0%B4%D0%B5%D0%BD%D1%82%D0%BE%D0%BC_%D0%AE%D0%90%D0%A0_%D0%94%D0%B6%D0%B5%D0%B9%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B1%D0%BE%D0%BC_%D0%97%D1%83%D0%BC%D0%BE%D0%B9_1.jpg)

Zuma greets Russian President [Vladimir Putin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Putin "Vladimir Putin") in 2015.

Zuma's administration pursued a number of structural economic policy reforms, but critics characterised them as "investor-unfriendly",[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Shipalana-2017-106) and most were met significant opposition. His reforms included the increased regulation of [private security companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_private_security_companies "List of private security companies").[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Shipalana-2017-106)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Mtyala-2015-114) He also increased the regulation of oil, gas, and minerals resources.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Shipalana-2017-106)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Harvey-2015-115) Furthermore, Zuma announced a proposal to increase [black economic empowerment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Economic_Empowerment "Black Economic Empowerment") ownership requirements in mines.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-116)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Nicolson-2017-117) In 2017, Zuma advanced a proposal for the introduction of a national [minimum wage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_wage "Minimum wage").[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-118)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-119)

Zuma was attentive to [land reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reform_in_South_Africa "Land reform in South Africa") issues throughout his second term, but from 2017 he emphasised his support for land expropriation without compensation.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-120)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Merten-2017-121)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-122) While opening the ANC's [54th National Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_National_Conference_of_the_African_National_Congress "54th National Conference of the African National Congress") in December 2017, he unilaterally announced that [higher education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education_in_South_Africa "Higher education in South Africa") would be free for students in households whose income was less than [R](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_rand "South African rand")350,000 per year, meeting a central demand of the [#FeesMustFall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FeesMustFall "FeesMustFall") student protests.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Mail_&_Guardian-2018-123)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-124)

South Africa's [social grants programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_welfare_programs_in_South_Africa "Social welfare programs in South Africa") expanded under Zuma,[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Shipalana-2017-106)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-125) and Zuma was praised for his HIV/AIDS policy which has been credited with increasing [life expectancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_expectancy "Life expectancy") in South Africa.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Shipalana-2017-106)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-126)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-127) However, his critics claim that his policies increased South Africa's debt burden[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Mail_&_Guardian-2018-123)[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Henderson-2018-128) with the [debt-to-GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debt-to-GDP_ratio "Debt-to-GDP ratio") ratio increasing from 28% at the start of his presidency[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-129) to just over 50% in the week of his resignation.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Henderson-2018-128)[Nedbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nedbank "Nedbank"), one of South Africa's largest banks, estimates that poor policy decisions, maladministration, and [corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corruption "Corruption") during Zuma's second term alone cost the South African economy R470 billion (US$33.7 billion).[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-130)

Contracts with the [consulting firms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consulting_firm "Consulting firm")[McKinsey & Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McKinsey_&_Company "McKinsey & Company"), [KPMG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KPMG "KPMG"), and [Deloitte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deloitte "Deloitte") were linked to alleged corruption in [state-owned enterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State-owned_enterprise "State-owned enterprise"). McKinsey & Company eventually reached an agreement with the South African government and paid back R1 Billion (US$67.3 million) for problems relating to work done at [Eskom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eskom "Eskom"), as well as a company linked to the [Gupta family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_family "Gupta family"). In January 2022 the South African government published the findings of an inquiry into [state capture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_capture "State capture") and the consultancy firm [Bain & Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bain_&_Company "Bain & Company") stands accused of helping Zuma to undermine the South African tax authority.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-131)

### Foreign policy

See also: [List of international presidential trips made by Jacob Zuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_international_presidential_trips_made_by_Jacob_Zuma "List of international presidential trips made by Jacob Zuma")

Zuma's first state visit as president was to [Angola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angola "Angola"), where he sought to improve relations with the government of President [José Eduardo dos Santos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Eduardo_dos_Santos "José Eduardo dos Santos"), who had had a tense relationship with Mbeki.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Landsberg-2012-90)[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Cilliers-2017-132) His government's [foreign policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_policy "Foreign policy") emphasised the [developmental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_development "Economic development") objectives of African and [Global South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_North_and_Global_South "Global North and Global South") countries[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Landsberg-2012-90) with a focus on [economic diplomacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_diplomacy "Economic diplomacy").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Landsberg-2012-90)[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Cilliers-2017-132)[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-133) It was also characterised by a pivot towards the [BRIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRIC_(economics_term) "BRIC (economics term)") countries, especially China.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Shipalana-2017-106)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Mpungose-2018-134)[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-135) In December 2010, South Africa became a formal member of the BRIC organisation, which was subsequently renamed [BRICS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRICS "BRICS"),[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-foreignpolicyjournal.com-136) and Zuma attended the group's [third summit meeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3rd_BRICS_summit "3rd BRICS summit") in [Sanya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanya "Sanya"), China, in 2011. South Africa's admission followed a concerted campaign for membership and has been described as "a huge diplomatic coup" and "the most important foreign policy achievement of the Zuma administration".[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Cilliers-2017-132)

Zuma speaks with [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") and [David Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Cameron "David Cameron") at a [G8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_of_Eight "Group of Eight") African Outreach meeting in 2010.

During South Africa's tenure on the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council"), Zuma's administration was criticised for deviating in its stance on certain foreign regimes, especially in its attitudes towards international intervention in [civil conflicts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_war "Civil war"). It voted in favour of [Resolution 1970](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_1970 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 1970") and [Resolution 1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_1973 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 1973") but condemned their use by the [North Atlantic Treaty Organisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO") (NATO) as the basis for [military intervention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_military_intervention_in_Libya "2011 military intervention in Libya") in [Libya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Libyan_Civil_War "First Libyan Civil War").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Landsberg-2012-90)[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-137) It also voted in favour of a 2012 resolution calling for Syrian President [Bashar al-Assad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bashar_al-Assad "Bashar al-Assad") to step down,[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-138) but established friendly relations with the Assad regime after the [2014 Syrian presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Syrian_presidential_election "2014 Syrian presidential election").[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-139)[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-140) The administration also appeared to vacillate in its response to the disputed [2010 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Ivorian_presidential_election "2010 Ivorian presidential election") in Côte d'Ivoire.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Landsberg-2012-90)

#### Zimbabwe

In Zimbabwe, Mbeki had advocated for non-confrontational "quiet diplomacy" as an alternative to the "megaphone diplomacy" used by Western governments that harshly criticised [Robert Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe "Robert Mugabe")'s regime.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-141) This approach was controversial, with elements of the ruling alliance calling for a tougher stance against Mugabe and the ruling [ZANU–PF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZANU%E2%80%93PF "ZANU–PF").[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-142)[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-143)[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-144) In a 2006 interview with _[Der Spiegel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der\_Spiegel "Der Spiegel")_, Zuma had supported quiet diplomacy and said of Mugabe:

> The Europeans often ignore the fact that Mugabe is very popular among Africans... The people love him. So how can we condemn him? Many in Africa believe that there is a racist aspect to European and American criticism of Mugabe. Millions of blacks died in Angola, the Republic of Congo and Rwanda. A few whites lost their lives in Zimbabwe, unfortunately, and already the West is bent out of shape.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-145)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/The_Prime_Minister%2C_Dr._Manmohan_Singh_interacting_with_the_President_of_South_Africa%2C_Mr._Jacob_Zuma%2C_at_the_G-20_Summit%2C_at_Pittsburgh%2C_USA_on_September_25%2C_2009.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Prime_Minister,_Dr._Manmohan_Singh_interacting_with_the_President_of_South_Africa,_Mr._Jacob_Zuma,_at_the_G-20_Summit,_at_Pittsburgh,_USA_on_September_25,_2009.jpg)

Zuma and Indian Prime Minister [Manmohan Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manmohan_Singh "Manmohan Singh") at the 2009 [G20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G20 "G20") summit

By December 2007, Zuma was more forthcoming in criticising Zimbabwe's leadership, contrasting his own policy to Mbeki's, and observing that it was "tragic that other world leaders who witness repression pretend it is not happening, or is exaggerated".[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-146) He was critical of the Zimbabwean government's behaviour during the disputed [March 2008 elections in Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Zimbabwean_general_election "2008 Zimbabwean general election") and called the delays "suspicious".[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-147)[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-148) In a press conference on 24 June he said, "We cannot agree with ZANU-PF. We cannot agree with them on values. We fought for the right of people to vote, we fought for democracy."[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-149) At an ANC dinner in July, he rebuked Mugabe for refusing to step down,[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-150) and in November he said that the [South African Development Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_African_Development_Community "Southern African Development Community") (SADC) should "force" Zimbabwean leaders to reach an agreement, if necessary.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-151)

In 2010, Zuma called for international sanctions against Mugabe and his allies to be lifted.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-152)[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-153) After a March 2013 meeting with Mugabe in [Pretoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretoria "Pretoria"), he highlighted the commonalities between his and Mugabe's political parties, telling the press, "We share the same values, we went through the same route... We believe that our positions as former liberation movements need to be consolidated."[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Drum-2013-154) Despite tensions in later months, as Zuma and SADC attempted to nudge Mugabe towards democratic reforms,[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-155) the _[Business Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business\_Day\_(South\_Africa) "Business Day (South Africa)")_ reported that relations between the countries remained "cordial" throughout Zuma's presidency.[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Matsabu-2017-156)

#### International Criminal Court

South Africa hosted the 25th Summit of the AU in [Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg "Johannesburg") from 7 to 15 June 2015. It was attended by Sudanese president [Omar al-Bashir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omar_al-Bashir "Omar al-Bashir"), then a fugitive from the [International Criminal Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Criminal_Court "International Criminal Court") (ICC), which sought to prosecute him on charges of [genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocide "Genocide") and [crimes against humanity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimes_against_humanity "Crimes against humanity"). South Africa was a signatory to the [Rome Statute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome_Statute "Rome Statute"), which obliged it to arrest al-Bashir, but instead granted him diplomatic immunity while he attended the summit.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-News24-2015b-157) While the matter was being adjudicated by a South African High Court, and just after Judge President [Dunstan Mlambo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunstan_Mlambo "Dunstan Mlambo") ordered al-Bashir's arrest, the state's lawyer told the court that he had left the country.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-News24-2015b-157) His plane left from [Waterkloof Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_Base_Waterkloof "Air Force Base Waterkloof"), presumably with the government's knowledge[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Cilliers-2017-132)[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-158) and reportedly with Zuma's explicit approval.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-159) When it was criticised for this breach, the South African government argued that the ICC was used unfairly against African heads of state while failing to hold Western leaders to the same standards.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Mpungose-2018-134)[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-160) In 2016, it announced in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") that it was withdrawing from the ICC,[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-161) and Zuma's administration subsequently tabled legislation to effect the withdrawal.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Fabricius-2019-162)

### Mandela's memorial

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Mandela-Memorial_8175.JPG/250px-Mandela-Memorial_8175.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mandela-Memorial_8175.JPG)

A jumbotron shows Zuma entering Mandela's memorial on 10 December 2013.

In a press conference on 5 December 2013, Zuma announced the death of Nelson Mandela, South Africa's first democratically elected president.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-163)[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-164) The memorial took place on 10 December 2013 at [FNB Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FNB_Stadium "FNB Stadium") near [Soweto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soweto "Soweto"). When Zuma entered the stadium parts of the crowd booed him loudly.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-165)[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-166) Ramaphosa and Archbishop [Desmond Tutu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Tutu "Desmond Tutu") called for discipline,[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Thelwell-2013-167)[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Mnyanda-2013-168) with Ramaphosa telling the crowd in Zulu that the country could address its internal disagreements when foreign dignitaries were not present.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Grootes-2013-169) Some South African commentators said that the crowd's actions were unexpected,[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Thelwell-2013-167)[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Grootes-2013-169) and they were widely linked to the ongoing [Nkandla scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nkandla_homestead "Nkandla homestead"),[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Thelwell-2013-167)[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Whitaker-2013-170)[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-171) a draft of the Public Protector's provisional report had been leaked the previous week, or to dissatisfaction with Zuma's administration more generally.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-172) Others suggested that the booing reflected frustration with the lack of socioeconomic change under the ANC government since Mandela's presidency,[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Whitaker-2013-170) or that it reflected enduring divisions within the ANC; the crowd also chanted Mbeki's name.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Grootes-2013-169) In a public statement, the ANC chastised those who had booed, saying they had embarrassed the country.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-Mnyanda-2013-168) The [South African Broadcasting Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Broadcasting_Corporation "South African Broadcasting Corporation") (SABC) was criticised for having cut away from the booing in its live broadcast of the memorial.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-173)

### Re-election

Despite an "[Anyone but Zuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anyone_but_Zuma "Anyone but Zuma")" campaign in the run-up to the ANC's [53rd National Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/53rd_National_Conference_of_the_African_National_Congress "53rd National Conference of the African National Congress"),[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-174)[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-175) Zuma was re-elected ANC president on 18 December 2012, beating Deputy President [Kgalema Motlanthe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kgalema_Motlanthe "Kgalema Motlanthe") by a large margin.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-cp2-176) Although in 2008 he had said that he would prefer to serve only one term as president,[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-177) Zuma became the ANC's sole presidential candidate in the [2014 national election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_South_African_general_election "2014 South African general election"). In January 2014, after he was heckled at Mandela's memorial, the _Sunday Tribune_ reported that around November 2013, KwaZulu-Natal branches of the ANC had discussed a proposed resolution asking Zuma not to run for a second term as the country's president.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-178) However, ANC Deputy Secretary General [Jessie Duarte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Duarte "Jessie Duarte") dismissed rumours of disunity in the ANC saying, "The policy is that the president of the ANC is always the candidate for the election. We don't have another candidate and there will be no other candidate."[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-179)

The ANC retained its majority in the national election, and on 21 May 2014, the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_of_South_Africa "National Assembly of South Africa") elected Zuma to a second term as president.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-180)

### Nkandla homestead

Zuma's [Nkandla homestead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nkandla_homestead "Nkandla homestead") in [KwaZulu-Natal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KwaZulu-Natal "KwaZulu-Natal")

Zuma began his second term amid ongoing controversy over what were officially security upgrades made with state funds to his [private homestead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nkandla_homestead "Nkandla homestead") at Nkandla. Public Protector [Thuli Madonsela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thuli_Madonsela "Thuli Madonsela") investigated, and in late November 2013 her draft report was leaked to the _Mail & Guardian._[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-mail2-181) Similar to the final version of the report, titled "Secure in Comfort" and released on 19 March 2014,[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-182) the draft found that some of the Nkandla upgrades exceeded Zuma's security needs and recommended that Zuma should repay the state.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-mail2-181) The opposition, Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), and DA applied for legal recourse to compel Zuma to follow the recommendations in Madonsela's report, and the [Constitutional Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_Court_of_South_Africa "Constitutional Court of South Africa") found in their favour on 31 March 2016. In _[EFF v Speaker; DA v Speaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic\_Freedom\_Fighters\_v\_Speaker\_of\_the\_National\_Assembly "Economic Freedom Fighters v Speaker of the National Assembly")_, the full court agreed that Madonsela's report was binding, meaning Zuma was required to repay the state for some of the Nkandla upgrades and that Zuma had failed to uphold the country's Constitution.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-183) In a public address on 1 April, Zuma welcomed the judgment and apologised to the country,[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-184) though legal academic [Pierre de Vos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_de_Vos "Pierre de Vos") said that the statement seriously misconstrued the judgment.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-185)[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Zuma#cite_note-186)
